newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rail freight traffic down in latest week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rail freight traffic down in latest week.

text.p: Floods in the Midwest and strikes in the automotive industry caused U.S. railroad freight traffic to fall in the week ended April 19 from the same week a year ago, the Association of American Railroads said Thursday.
Carloads and ton-miles fell while intermodal traffic, which does not include carloads, rose in the latest week, the AAR reported.

AAR said carload traffic fell 1.2 percent to 344,889 in the April 19 week from 348,962 last year. Ton-miles fell 1.5 percent to 26.2 billion in the latest week from 26.6 billion last year. A ton-mile equals one ton of freight hauled one mile.
AAR attributed the drop in traffic to the floods in the Midwest and to strikes at automobile plants.
"Flooding in the Midwest continued to affect rail traffic," AAR Senior Assistant Vice President Craig Rockey said. "Scattered automotive strikes also had an effect."

The biggest drop in carload freight was felt in nonmetallic minerals, which dropped 19.1 percent to 8,422 carloads from 10,407 last year. Grain carloads also plummeted, falling 18.1 percent to 22,791 from 27,838 last year.
AAR said intermodal traffic in the week totaled 167,706 trailers and containers, up 7.8 percent from 155,612 in the year-earlier week.

The biggest increases in carload freight from a year ago were in petroleum products, which rose 7.5 percent to 5,702 carloads, from 5,305, chemicals, which rose 6.8 percent to 32,873, from 30,786, and lumber and wood products, which rose 6.5 percent to 6,049, from 5,678.

In the first 16 weeks of 1997, AAR said intermodal traffic rose six percent from the same period in 1996. Ton-miles rose three percent while carloads increased 2.4 percent from the same 1996 period, it said.

AAR also said carloads on the two U.S.-owned railroads based in Canada totaled 24,821 trailers and containers, up seven percent from the year-earlier week, while carloads totaled 58,481, up 2.1 percent from a year ago.

Combined total volume in the United States and Canada for the first 16 weeks was 6.2 million carloads, up 2.1 percent from the same 1996 period, while intermodal traffic totaled 2.93 million trailers and containers, up 6.4 percent, AAR said.
